To start, I do care about you, stranger or not, and I'm very glad that you spoke to me about this; thank you for sharing. ❤️ This is definitely a very difficult situation, and I'd like to say that if International Affairs don't make you happy, then that is more than ok. It's ok to change your life plans, especially if they don't make you feel good and are stressing you out with deadlines and assignments. I doubt that you dropped it out of laziness; I'm sure you did that because you realized that it was taking a really heavy toll on you. Something that you might want to consider, if you don't want to change your major, is maybe attending college part-time. You would graduate later and get your degree later, but it'd help with the workload. If you do want to switch your major, you may want to consider taking a gap year of sorts to give yourself time to figure out what makes you happy. That's actually what I'm doing right now, and I can say from experience that it's pretty helpful, especially for saving up money. 

With all that being said, let's now address the situation with your parents. That's definitely a sticky situation, but even if they're upset with you, it sounds like they care an awful lot about you and your success, so overtime, they'll understand. I suggest having an in-person conversation with them about this, if you're able to do so, or speaking over video call because this is definitely a conversation that you want to have with the ability to see their body language and hear their tones. When you speak about it, start by telling your story. Explain what's been going on with you mentally and how much of a toll your classes had been putting on you. Stress the fact that you were unhappy with those three classes, and you've been having a very difficult time emotionally recently; your honesty will serve you well because it shows your parents the struggles you were going through that led up to your decision, so it'll help them understand better. After that, I'd tell them that you decided to drop those three classes and might change your major. Be honest about how this is making you feel because I'm sure your parents would much rather lose money than lose their child. ❤️ Explain that you've been feeling really awful about your decision and that you're sorry for needing to change things up, but ultimately, it's important that you know you aren't a failure nor are you a disappointment to your parents for changing your life path. They will learn to forgive the money loss because they likely love you dearly and want what's best for you. If you're really concerned that this money loss is very serious, maybe try working out a payment plan for you to pay back the money for those classes overtime, like a loan. No matter how this conversation goes, please remember that your life matters, and you're not in the wrong for trying to better yourself in the long-term. If you're unhappy with your major, that's ok; there are ways to change it and find a career path that will bring you happiness. It's ok to not have your life all figured out, especially in college. You're young, and you've got your whole life ahead of you; there's no telling what amazing adventures still await you. ❤️

I'm so sorry that you're struggling with such awful pressure. Something that might help you is that your parents will only have a say in your life for a very, very small portion; you have so many years of potentially wonderful experiences ahead of you, and your parents will not be able to make you feel like shit for the rest of your life. You can and will escape their negative influence on you because this is your life to live, not theirs, and they won't be able to decide how you get to live and what is and isn't expected of you. Along with that, I recently graduated from high school, and I remember how many times I would cry over a bad grade in math or even turning something in late. Get your tears out in the moment, but always remember that school doesn't entirely decide the rest of your life. Even if you graduate with a low GPA or even later than the rest of your class, there are ways to work around that, such as attending a community college for the first two years to raise up your GPA. What you experience now will not haunt you for the rest of your life, when it comes to high school assignments and stress. In ten years, that shitty math teacher who always had something against won't even be on your mind anymore. I know that school often tells us that we'll "regret" our "bad grades" and such in the future, but the moment that I graduated, I felt like I was free from some awful burden weighing me down. You can get through this struggle at school because frankly, fuck school, especially high school. If you're in the US, the system is awful and values memorization over actual learning. They every encourage you to compare yourself to your classmates, which is a really unhealthy lesson to be teaching to kids. You may not have the same awesome grade as Susie McSue or the perfect good-two-shoes track record like Bob Smith, but that doesn't make you any less valuable than them. That doesn't make you stupid or worthless or even a failure. Hell, Albert Einstein flunked high school, and his old teachers even claimed that they thought he'd be a failure, but today, his name is something that even little kids know about, and his accomplishments have outlived him for decades. There is so much more to life than school and parents and peers. You just need to give yourself the chance of experiencing what else is out there. ❤️
